Situation1: They are asked to take part in an important family event like a holiday celebration or trip.
Expectation2: Challenge unfair systems and influence policy change
Situation2: They raise concerns about a policy that seems to disadvantage certain youth, seniors, or refugee applicants.
Story: I stared at my phone, my sister’s message glowing on the screen: “Don’t forget, we need you at the family dinner this weekend. It means a lot to Mom.” I could almost hear her voice, warm but insistent, reminding me how much these gatherings matter, especially since Dad’s health started to decline. I wanted to be there, to laugh with them, to show I cared. But my mind kept drifting to the email from the advocacy group—there was a last-minute meeting scheduled at the same time as the dinner. We were preparing to challenge a new policy that would make it even harder for refugee youth to access support. I’d promised to speak, to use my voice for those who couldn’t. My family expected me to show up, to be present, to be a good brother. But the people I advocated for needed me too, and I knew how much was at stake. The weight of both expectations pressed down on me, my heart pulled in two directions, each side demanding all of me. I sat there, torn, unable to move, knowing I couldn’t be in both places at once.
